current.descent_text: The Southwest Face (East Peak's low-fifth-class line) is short — 2 pitches — and the standard descent is to rappel the route itself: three rappel stations are encountered descending the line, using natural anchors (slings around the chockstone/horns typical of this rock, not bolts) rather than fixed hardware. You do not rappel from the summit block itself: parties protect the short scramble down from it to the top station with a handline, and there is a further rappel station down in the approach gully used to regain packs. The first two rappels go on a single rope, but the last is a full double-rope rappel needing two 70 m ropes — a single 60 m rope will not complete this descent, and 70 m ropes are what parties who have done it recommend. Bring an extra sling or two since anchor material on featureless granite here tends to be climber-placed webbing that may need refreshing. The final rappel lands back past the chockstone into the North-East Peak notch/gully, from which you downclimb and scramble the loose gully back down to the basin above Lake Ingalls, retracing the approach. Watch for loose rock in this gully on the way down, especially if other parties are above. As an alternative some climbers skip rappelling the direct line and instead do a short 4th-class downclimb from the East Peak summit block to link into the main peak's South Ridge descent/rappel line (shared with the standard Ingalls Peak South Ridge route), then talus back to Lake Ingalls.

current.rappels: No fixed anchors — every rappel station must be built and left. Carry cord and spare nuts specifically for retreat; double ropes make a retreat much less committing. The normal descent is a scramble off the north side, not a rappel line.
current.descent_text: From the false summit, downclimb exposed, broken ridge terrain, then work down a loose, sandy ledge system into Avalanche Canyon; traverse the canyon back around to the Home Lake cirque to close the loop. The first-ascent party's round trip (climb plus this descent) took about 12.5 hours.

current.rappels: There is no East Ridge descent. 14 single-rope rappels with a 60-70 m rope: 5 down the upper West Ridge, a scramble down to a notch, then 9 down the South Face to the Terror Glacier. With two ropes, parties have instead made seven double-rope rappels straight down the West Ridge.
current.rappel_count_note: The descent is the same as the West Ridge and South Face routes’. Counted for one 60-70 m rope, which is what most parties now carry: 5 rappels on the upper West Ridge and 9 on the South Face below the notch. The stations are spaced for a single rope. With two ropes, parties have descended the whole West Ridge in seven double-rope rappels off natural anchors instead, skipping the South Face. Anchors on the ridge were reported rebuilt in June 2024, but stations vary and some are tattered, so carry cord to back them up. Two landmarks on the ridge part of the line: a large horn anchor, and a fixed three-pin anchor where the rappel goes down and climber’s right off a large overhang and hangs free, with the next station offset rather than straight below.

current.descent_text: There is no established East Ridge descent — the standard way down combines two other routes: parties downclimb/rappel the upper West Ridge crest, then continue down Inspiration's South Face to regain the Terror Glacier, essentially the same descent used by West Ridge climbers (the East Ridge is reported as distinctly poorer, looser rock for descending, so nobody down-climbs it). Parties describe on the order of 5 rappels down the upper West Ridge followed by a scramble to a notch and roughly 9 more rappels down the South Face (about 12-14 total), typically on a single 60-70m rope, using a mix of fixed slings/rap stations of variable quality (back these up) and natural gear anchors. Some parties instead run the full West Ridge on a doubled rope, taking around 7 longer double-rope rappels off natural nut/cam anchors and skipping the separate South Face section. Expect a long free-hanging rappel or two, rockfall-prone traversing stations, and the need to re-rope for glacier travel immediately upon reaching the Terror Glacier at the bottom before reversing the approach back to camp and out the Goodell Creek boot path/trail — this exit is long enough that parties commonly finish it after dark.

current.descent_text: The standard descent from the summit goes down the West Ridge crest itself, then finishes down Inspiration's South Face — it is not a walk-off. Most recent parties (e.g. a well-documented July 2024 ascent) report roughly 5 rappels down the upper West Ridge on a single 60-70m rope, using a mix of fixed slings/rap rings left by prior parties (quality varies — some stations have been found tattered and worth backing up or replacing) and natural nut/cam anchors built on the spot. After the ridge raps, parties briefly stow the rope and downclimb/scramble 3rd-4th class terrain to a notch, from which roughly 9 more single-rope rappels descend the South Face to the Terror Glacier, for a total in the neighborhood of 12-14 rappels overall — the final rappel often takes the full length of the doubled rope to reach flat glacier snow. Some parties instead descend the full length of the West Ridge on a doubled/twin-rope system, using longer double-rope rappels off natural gear (solid nut placements) to cut the total rappel count to around 7, bypassing the separate South Face section — either line is used depending on party preference and rope setup. Watch for loose, rockfall-prone rock on the traversing stations (some raps go sideways, not straight down, to reach the next anchor and to dodge fall lines), stay alert for hard-to-spot anchor stations, and re-rope for glacier travel the instant you're back on the Terror Glacier at the bottom. From the glacier, reverse the approach: back across the crevassed glacier and slabs to Terror Basin camp, then down the steep boot path and Goodell Creek Trail to the trailhead — parties frequently finish this exit in the dark, with some trip reports noting arrival at camp or the car well after nightfall.

current.descent_text: Standard descent rappels the upper West Ridge to a notch, then continues down the South Face to the glacier rather than reversing the Great Gash. From the summit, downclimb/scramble a few hundred feet toward a notch on the ridge, then begin rappelling. Multiple trip reports of this exact route confirm it as a sustained multi-rappel descent through a gully/notch system with no bolts; the stations are fixed pins, nuts and cord of variable quality, slung horns, or anchors built from gear (nuts, small-to-medium cams), so carry a rack sufficient for both the climb and for leaving/building rappel anchors, plus some cord or rap tat. One detailed trip report of this route logged 7 double-rope rappels, about three and a half down the West Ridge and four down the South Face, back to the Terror Glacier, building a fresh natural anchor at each station; a separate party descending the same general line but counting differently (single 70m rope, more, shorter pitches) reported roughly 5 rappels down the upper West Ridge to a notch followed by about 9 more rappels down through the gully/South Face terrain to the glacier, with several rappels traversing hard to one side to reach the next station and the final rappel using nearly the full rope length to reach a flat spot on the ice. Two ropes give the fewest rappels. The two-rope stations sit roughly 60 m apart and a single 70 m rope doubled reaches only about 35 m, so on one rope expect roughly twice as many stations: about 14 rappels of 30-35 m, which is what the single-rope party above ended up doing. Expect loose rock in the gully and real risk of the rope hanging up on the traversing raps, so back up rappels and check pulls carefully. The descent ends back on the Terror Glacier at the base of the West Ridge/South Face, from which you re-cross the icefall (same crevasse hazard as the approach, now on tired legs and possibly softer afternoon snow) to regain camp, then reverse the Terror Basin boot path and Goodell Creek Trail to the trailhead.

current.rappels: Rappel the route (~16 raps from bolted anchors on all pitches but P15); much of the wall overhangs, so many rappels swing significantly or need a directional piece left to reach the next station cleanly; expect to down-aid a long section of P7 if no fixed line was left in place
current.rappel_count_note: Rappel the route, one rappel per pitch: every pitch has a bolted stainless-steel anchor except pitch 15, whose gear belay has a bolted rappel anchor along the ledge to the right. Pitch lengths are not published, so no rappel lengths are given; bring two ropes. Much of the wall overhangs, so plan on directional pieces or swinging in to reach stations, and on fixing or down-aiding pitch 7. The first-ascent party descended unconventionally, one climber riding the haul bags down roughly 1,000-1,200 ft before the rest finished with double-rope rappels, which is not a plan for a repeat.

rappel_detail.anchor: bolted/stainless-steel anchor

hazards: arriving at the gear belay and looking for bolts that are not there is the trap on this station
rappel_detail.station: Pitch 15 is the one pitch without a bolted belay - the belay is gear, on a large ledge. The bolted rappel anchor is set far to the right along that ledge as you face the wall, not at the belay, so walk the ledge to find it.

rappel_detail.pull: Strip any lines fixed during the ascent on the way down; leaving them is discouraged here and the buttress already carries old rope from previous attempts that should not be trusted.
rappel_detail.notes: Final rappel to the base; remove any fixed lines left during the ascent as an established leave-no-trace practice on this route.
rappel_detail.anchor: bolted/stainless-steel anchor

current.descent_text: The descent is accomplished by rappelling the route in full. Due to the sustained overhanging terrain throughout most pitches, careful anchor placement is critical, particularly on pitches with significant roofs. Climbers should plan to use at least two ropes for rappelling. The first ascent team used an unconventional technique where one climber managed haul bags on a very long rappel before the remaining climbers rappelled in pairs off stainless steel anchors. Plan to remove fixed lines during descent to preserve the rock.
